description: Tooth injuries are the most common facial injuries in children. When a parent should talk to a lawyer, and the unique legal issues in child dental claims.
shortAnswer: It really does depend: ask where, how and when the injury occurred. In general, if your child was injured and you feel it was due to someone else's negligence or lack of supervision, you should call me. Anytime you sense a cover up, it is important to contact an attorney so that a sifting investigation can take place.

faq.q: Can an injury to a child's baby tooth affect the permanent teeth?
faq.a: Baby teeth help shape the mouth for the permanent teeth and help guide the adult teeth into position. If your child loses teeth (or has damaged teeth) the permanent teeth are more likely to overlap or not come in at all. Also, an impact to a baby tooth can lead to the death of a permanent tooth.

faq.q: Will a dentist put a child's knocked-out baby tooth back in?
faq.a: A knocked out tooth (dentists call this an "avulsed" tooth) typically will not be put back in (called replanting). This is because attempts to replant a baby tooth can actually damage the permanent tooth that is growing inside of the bone.

faq.q: Why does it matter how much time has passed since my child's tooth injury?
faq.a: It is best to start collecting legal and medical documentation as soon as practicable after an injury, and the more time that passes the harder it gets for your doctor to address the all-important issue of causation. Causation has to do with making sure the dental records clearly link the cause of the injury to the injury.

faq.q: What if the dentist can't treat my young child's knocked-out tooth right away?
faq.a: Sometimes the dentist can't do anything for your child right away, particularly in the case of a knocked out tooth in a very young child. For my clients, presenting their legal claim to the insurance company was complicated by the reality that the future dental expenses were going to be the most significant part of their claim.
